experiment_plans.feasibility_notes: The hypothesis requires real-world weather station data with both rich and scarce station histories, but no such dataset exists among those listed. The closest match is uci_air_quality_hourly.csv, which contains hourly environmental measurements but lacks the required structure of distinct weather stations with varying data richness. To make this feasible, we will simplify the hypothesis to use a synthetic dataset simulating weather station data with known transfer learning properties, allowing us to test the core idea without real-world constraints.
experiment_plans.objective: To determine whether transfer learning from a data-rich synthetic weather station to a data-scarce station improves 24-hour temperature forecasting accuracy as measured by mean absolute error (MAE) compared to a baseline model trained solely on the data-scarce station's history.

dependent: mean absolute error (MAE) of temperature forecast

experiment_plans.design: A comparative benchmark experiment where two models are trained: one baseline model trained exclusively on the data-scarce station's historical data, and one transfer learning model that first trains on the data-rich station's data and then fine-tunes on the data-scarce station's data. The MAE of both models' 24-hour temperature forecasts is compared.

data_requirements.description: Synthetic weather station data generated to simulate two stations with different data richness levels. One station has abundant historical temperature data (rich), while another has limited historical data (scarce). This allows for controlled testing of transfer learning effectiveness.
preprocessing_steps: Generate synthetic time series data for two weather stations with different lengths of historical records
Ensure the rich station has at least 5 years of hourly temperature data
Ensure the scarce station has less than 1 year of hourly temperature data
Add realistic noise and seasonal patterns to mimic real-world conditions
Split each station's data into train/validation/test sets appropriately

methods.name: Transfer Learning
methods.description: A model is first pre-trained on data from a data-rich source station, then fine-tuned on data from a data-scarce target station to adapt to the new domain while leveraging learned features from the source.

methods.name: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
methods.description: An LSTM network is used as the forecasting model architecture due to its ability to capture temporal dependencies in time-series data, suitable for weather forecasting tasks.

methods.name: Fine-tuning
methods.description: After initial training on the rich station data, the model weights are adjusted using gradient descent on the scarce station data to adapt to the new domain.

evaluation.baseline: Model trained exclusively on the data-scarce station's historical data
evaluation.success_criteria: If the transfer learning model achieves lower MAE than the baseline model, the hypothesis is supported. If the MAE is higher or similar, the hypothesis is refuted.

implementation_steps.description: Generate synthetic weather station data with two stations: one with rich data (5+ years) and one with scarce data (<1 year). Save as CSV files with columns: timestamp, temperature, station_id.
Preprocess the data by normalizing temperature values, creating lagged features for time-series modeling, and splitting into train/validation/test sets for both stations.
Implement an LSTM-based forecasting model architecture with configurable input sequence length and hidden units.
Train the baseline model on the scarce station's data alone, saving the model weights after training completion.
Train the transfer learning model by first initializing with pre-trained weights from the rich station's model, then fine-tuning on the scarce station's data.
Evaluate both models on the test set of the scarce station using MAE as the primary metric, recording the results for statistical comparison.
Compare the MAE scores between the baseline and transfer learning models to determine if transfer learning improves forecasting accuracy.

risks: Synthetic data may not accurately reflect real-world variability and thus fail to validate the hypothesis
Inadequate preprocessing steps might lead to poor model performance in either case
Overfitting during fine-tuning phase could skew results toward the transfer learning approach
